segments.title: Why the Nile may outrank Trafalgar
segments.body: The Nile is both a warning against immobilizing a fleet in harbor and an unusually complete naval annihilation. A ship's defensive advantage begins with mobility, while anchorage restricts maneuver and may prevent guns from firing toward nearby infrastructure or civilians. The Battle of Navarino in 1827 shows that later fleets had still not absorbed that warning fully. France entered with thirteen ships of the line and four frigates but emerged with only two of each, crippling its Mediterranean freedom of action. The battle falls between the formal coalition wars: the expedition grew from the First Coalition's failed amphibious strategy, while its destruction helped define the Second Coalition before that war formally began. The Nile eliminated most of the deployed French force, and its long-term consequences may outrank Trafalgar's.

evidence.note: The transcript compares the Nile with Trafalgar, explains harbor vulnerability, and summarizes the French fleet's destruction.

segments.summary: The opening argues that the Battle of the Nile mattered more to the wider war than Nelson's more famous victory at Trafalgar.

segments.title: Failed invasion plans redirect France toward Egypt
segments.body: The Egyptian expedition continued the First Coalition's repeated attempts to use amphibious power against Britain. That earlier strategy included the Glorious First of June and the failed landing at Fishguard, where poor access routes, nearby fortifications, and a hostile local population made the chosen landing area especially weak. Once direct invasion appeared impractical against a stronger Royal Navy, French planners looked for an indirect way to damage British power. India became the recurring strategic target, with Egypt imagined as the route toward either the Red Sea or Syria. The change of destination did not remove the underlying naval problem because the army would still depend on maritime communications.

evidence.note: The transcript connects First Coalition amphibious operations, Fishguard, Royal Navy strength, and the turn toward India through Egypt.

segments.summary: French failures to cross the Channel turn an amphibious war against Britain into an indirect expedition toward Egypt and India.

segments.title: Perrée offers a French alternative to Villeneuve
segments.body: The Battle of the Malta Convoy in February 1800 provides a brief look ahead to the death of Jean-Baptiste Perrée. Perrée may have been the closest French equivalent to Cuthbert Collingwood rather than to Nelson. That comparison supports a command counterfactual: Perrée might have achieved more in later strategic command than Pierre-Charles Villeneuve was equipped to do. His death also narrowed France's already shallow pool of experienced senior officers.

evidence.note: The transcript identifies Perrée's death at the Malta Convoy and compares his unrealized command potential with Villeneuve and Collingwood.

segments.summary: The 1800 Battle of the Malta Convoy kills Jean-Baptiste Perrée, who may have been better suited to fleet command than Villeneuve.

segments.title: Napoleon's Egyptian expedition and its logistics trap
segments.body: The proposed expedition sought an indirect way to damage Britain after a cross-Channel invasion proved impractical. An army moving through Egypt, Syria, or toward India would still need ammunition, uniforms, food, and maritime support. Reaching India would also mean confronting the East India Company's well-drilled and reliably paid forces rather than simply entering an undefended possession. The plan therefore rested on naval communications that France could not reliably protect.

evidence.note: The transcript outlines the India strategy and the expedition's dependence on vulnerable maritime logistics.

segments.summary: Napoleon's route toward Egypt and India depended on sea supply lines that the stronger Royal Navy was positioned to sever.

segments.title: St Vincent holds Toulon while Nelson hunts
segments.body: John Jervis does not chase personally because the strategically larger threat remains inside Toulon. By maintaining the blockade, he prevents reinforcements and supplies from following Napoleon while Nelson searches with a detached squadron. Nelson had become a rear admiral only the previous year, but Jervis trusts his proven aggressiveness enough to give him the independent pursuit. Promotion depended on more than formal seniority: sea service, Admiralty favor, and available assignments could accelerate or obstruct an officer's rise. Promotion as a rear admiral of the yellow could formally advance an unwanted officer while effectively ending his active service. Jervis's blockade combines theater-level restraint with Nelson's calculated aggression at the point of contact.

evidence.note: The transcript explains why Jervis remains off Toulon and delegates the pursuit to Nelson.

segments.summary: Admiral St Vincent keeps the larger French force contained at Toulon while sending his most aggressive deputy after the expedition.

segments.title: The French convoy slips through to Malta and Egypt
segments.body: Napoleon's force expands as it moves through Genoa, Corsica, and Malta, but its dispersal and uncertain reports repeatedly create risks. When reports place Nelson nearby, Napoleon sends ships to investigate and temporarily weakens the convoy he is trying to protect. Nelson comes within roughly sixty nautical miles without making contact, illustrating the difficulty of maritime reconnaissance before modern communications. A fleet's apparent course could also mislead observers because sailing ships might steer for favorable wind rather than directly toward their destination. The French land successfully in Egypt, yet remain dependent on the fleet for their supply line.

evidence.note: The transcript follows the convoy route, seizure of Malta, failed contact with Nelson, and arrival at Alexandria.

segments.summary: The expedition collects transports, captures Malta, and reaches Alexandria while both fleets struggle with incomplete information.

segments.title: Malta falls, then HMS Seahorse captures Sensible
segments.body: The Knights of St John restrict the French fleet to two ships at a time because admitting the whole convoy would surrender control of the harbor. Napoleon answers by landing troops at seven places, while the order is weakened when many of its French members refuse to fight their countrymen. He secures Malta's fortifications, stores, artillery, and local armed forces after limited resistance. Soon afterward HMS Seahorse captures the French frigate Sensible on its voyage from Malta to Toulon. The prize carries treasure, wounded soldiers, and a senior officer from the defense of Malta, turning routine frigate warfare into a source of operational intelligence about the expedition.

evidence.note: The transcript describes the Knights' restriction, the French landings and surrender terms, and HMS Seahorse capturing Sensible with treasure and wounded personnel.

segments.summary: Napoleon forces the Knights Hospitaller to surrender Malta, but a British frigate soon captures a French vessel carrying treasure, wounded troops, and news of the conquest.

segments.title: Brueys anchors in the exposed Aboukir Bay
segments.body: Brueys prefers orders and security, while Nelson is willing to take calculated risks. Rear Admiral Blanquet argues that the fleet would be safer cruising at sea, but Alexandria cannot hold both the warships and transports. Bonaparte intends the fleet to move toward Corfu, yet the message is intercepted before it reaches Brueys. The admiral therefore remains at Aboukir Bay as though any bay must provide defensible shelter. In practice the broad indentation offers open water and insufficient protection between the head of the French line and shore.

evidence.note: The transcript profiles Brueys and criticizes Aboukir Bay as an exposed, poorly chosen fleet anchorage.

segments.summary: A cautious French commander chooses an anchorage that offers the appearance of protection without closing the fleet's vulnerable flank.

segments.title: The opposing fleets: French weight versus British depth
segments.body: Nelson's force is built mostly around 74-gun ships, without a first-rate, while the French line includes three 80-gun ships and the 120-gun Orient. On paper that gives France a meaningful firepower advantage. French personnel weakness predated the Revolution: the expulsion of the Huguenots had removed officers from a community that treated naval service as an important path into public life. Later political purges removed still more experienced officers, preventing Brueys from turning material strength into coordinated combat power.

evidence.note: The transcript inventories both fleets and contrasts French gun weight with British personnel and command quality.

segments.summary: France has heavier ships and greater theoretical broadside weight, but Britain brings a more cohesive corps of captains and trained crews.

segments.title: Leander defies the fourth-rate's usual restraint
segments.body: Most of Nelson's line consists of 74-gun third-rates, making Captain Thomas Thompson's 50-gun HMS Leander the conspicuous exception. Age-of-sail custom usually kept frigates from firing on ships of the line because a return broadside could destroy them. A similar practical restraint kept a fourth-rate from challenging a first-rate, even though it was not a formal immunity. Thompson disregards that disparity and later drives Leander into positions between French 80- and 120-gun ships. Leander's double rake is an unusually aggressive use of a nominally outclassed vessel.

evidence.note: The transcript identifies Leander as the fleet's 50-gun fourth-rate and explains the customary restraint between unequal ship types.
The transcript follows Leander into a double-raking position between much heavier French ships.

segments.summary: A 50-gun fourth-rate enters a battle dominated by 74s and refuses the practical restraint that normally kept smaller warships away from first-rates.

segments.title: Grounded Culloden still protects the attack
segments.body: Captain Thomas Troubridge drives HMS Culloden onto a shoal while pressing into Aboukir Bay in darkness. Lieutenant Thomas Hardy, commanding the sloop HMS Mutine, spends much of the action helping the stranded ship rather than joining the gun battle. Leander briefly tries to assist before abandoning the attempt and continuing where her firepower can matter more. When Alexander and Swiftsure arrive later, Culloden's people signal and shout warnings that steer them away from the shoal and into the fight. Although Culloden fires no broadside, its warnings still protect the attack, while Hardy's work precedes his appointment as Nelson's new flag captain.

evidence.note: The transcript introduces Culloden's grounding, Hardy's work from Mutine, and his later appointment as flag captain.
The transcript describes Leander abandoning an unsuccessful attempt to help Culloden and continuing into battle.
The transcript describes Troubridge and Culloden warning Alexander and Swiftsure away from the shoal.

segments.summary: Hardy works to free grounded Culloden while Troubridge warns late-arriving ships away from the same shoal.

segments.title: Nelson reaches Egypt too early and misses the convoy
segments.body: Nelson correctly guesses Egypt as the expedition's destination but reaches Alexandria before the French convoy and finds no enemy there. His better-drilled crews have driven their ships so effectively that the pursuit overshoots its target. The near miss creates a consequential counterfactual: an interception during unloading or at sea might have captured Napoleon and much of his army. The closing question sharpens the scenario into a night battle against both the French warships and their vulnerable transports before the expedition reaches Egypt. No fixed outcome is claimed, but French operational performance may not have been much better than it proved at Aboukir Bay. Superior mobility still fails to produce contact when reconnaissance and communications do not reveal the enemy's exact position.

evidence.note: The transcript explains that Nelson arrived at Alexandria before the convoy and considers the consequences of intercepting Napoleon's transports at sea.
The closing audience prompt asks how a night interception of the fleet and transports before Egypt might have changed the campaign.

segments.summary: Superior British sailing carries Nelson to Alexandria before the French arrive, creating a narrow missed chance to catch Napoleon's transports at sea.

segments.title: Nelson plans to double the anchored French line
segments.body: The intended maneuver deprives the anchored French ships of the protection they expect from their landward side. It also concentrates multiple British broadsides against successive parts of the French line. Competent preparation would have closed the shoreward gap, secured internal openings, and readied the landward battery even if an attack seemed unlikely from that direction. The plan therefore depends on initiative by individual British captains and on French failure to take those precautions.

evidence.note: The transcript explains Nelson's plan to break and attack the French line from both sides.

segments.summary: Nelson's captains understand a plan to break the line, pass between the French and shore, and attack each ship from both sides.

segments.title: Suffren provides the counterpoint to France's naval nadir
segments.body: In this interpretation, the Nile was the French Navy's qualitative low point rather than evidence of permanent national inferiority at sea. Pierre-André de Suffren provides the counterpoint, representing the service at its qualitative best. Royal Navy opponents respected Suffren so strongly that "the Admiral" could identify him without further explanation. The comparison separates the institutional damage of a particular era from the abilities French officers and crews had demonstrated under stronger leadership.

evidence.note: The transcript calls the Nile France's qualitative naval low point and contrasts it with Royal Navy respect for Suffren as “the Admiral.”

segments.summary: Royal Navy opponents called Pierre-André de Suffren "the Admiral," a sharp contrast with the French Navy's weakness at the Nile.

segments.title: British night-fighting preparation meets French delay
segments.body: The British use illuminated ensigns and mast lights to reduce the danger of friendly fire, while springs on anchor cables will let them aim after anchoring. Brueys has sent about a third of his personnel ashore to forage after the army stripped fleet stores, and local Bedouin attacks force him to commit still more men as escorts. His frigates have not been deployed as a scouting screen, so the French discover the British approach late and struggle to count the ships correctly. The French then redistribute frigate crews among unfamiliar ships of the line, weakening vessels that should have served as scouts and signal repeaters. Brueys misreads Nelson's temporary slowing as evidence that the attack will wait until morning, leaving French captains gathered aboard Orient as the danger closes.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts British night-action measures with French manpower shortages, meetings, and misreading of Nelson's approach.

segments.summary: Recognition lights, anchor springs, and delegated initiative prepare Nelson's ships for darkness while Brueys holds a captains' conference.

segments.title: Brueys reports his weakness but does not change the fleet's position
segments.body: Brueys had already warned the French marine minister that his crews were weak in number and quality and that much of the rigging needed repair. Yet he describes these hazards without using his authority to choose a safer position or operating method. When Nelson slows to assemble his approaching ships, Brueys interprets the pause as proof that no attack will come until morning. The British commander assumes his opponent may act intelligently, while the French commander projects his own reluctance onto Nelson and continues the conference aboard Orient.

evidence.note: The transcript quotes Brueys on weak crews and rigging, criticizes his lack of agency, and contrasts the two admirals' readings of Nelson's approach.

segments.summary: The French admiral recognizes poor crews and damaged rigging, yet treats those conditions as fixed while a captains' conference consumes the time needed to sail or prepare.

segments.title: Goliath finds the gap behind the French van
segments.body: Goliath and Zealous continue taking soundings rather than being distracted by a French decoy frigate. Nelson briefly consults pilots seized from Alexandrian vessels, then lets other ships pass Vanguard so the fleet does not lose momentum. Captain Thomas Foley recognizes the opening at the head of the anchored line and immediately executes Nelson's shoreward attack. Double-shotting costs roughly a third of normal range, but at pistol-shot distance it sends two projectiles through the target with each discharge. Goliath's prepared guns, Royal Marines, and a company of Austrian grenadiers exploit that close range while French captains are still returning from their conference. Accounts differ on how the Austrian contingent came aboard, so that detail remains unresolved.

evidence.note: The transcript explains double-shotting's range penalty and close-range destructive effect.
The transcript describes soundings, discovery of the gap, the first British ships passing inside the French line, and differing accounts of how the Austrian grenadiers came aboard Goliath.

segments.summary: Soundings and inaccurate French fire reveal enough water for Foley to pass between the leading French ship and shore.

segments.title: The French van is attacked from both sides
segments.body: Orion disables the frigate Sérieuse with a single close-range broadside, while Theseus, Audacious, and Vanguard take stations around the leading French ships. French crews prepared mainly for attack from seaward and cannot man both batteries effectively. Better British drill and roughly twice the firing rate multiply the effect of concentrating two ships against one. The untouched French rear does not move forward to relieve the van, allowing the British to defeat successive sections instead of fighting the whole line at once.

evidence.note: The transcript follows the British entry on both sides and explains the resulting fire-rate and concentration advantage.

segments.summary: Successive British ships enter on both sides of the French van, creating local superiority and rolling the engagement down the line.

segments.title: Theseus disguises a 74 as a first-rate
segments.body: HMS Theseus is a 74-gun third-rate painted to resemble a first-rate at a distance. The Royal Navy sometimes used this visual deception to make an observing enemy overcount the fleet's largest ships. At the Nile, Theseus backs the appearance with aggressive handling, crosses Guerrier's bow, and takes a shoreward station against Spartiate. The French ship has concentrated its available crew on the seaward battery and is unprepared to answer the attack from landward. The deception works alongside the decentralized initiative needed to execute Nelson's double envelopment.

evidence.note: The transcript explains Theseus's first-rate paint scheme and follows the ship into its shoreward attack on Spartiate.

segments.summary: A deceptive paint scheme makes HMS Theseus look like a first-rate before the 74-gun ship joins the attack inside the French line.

segments.title: Leander rakes the line as French losses mount
segments.body: Leander crosses positions from which its prepared batteries can fire along French hulls on both sides. Because both broadsides were loaded before entering the action, the 50-gun ship can rake different French targets to port and starboard as gaps open. At the head of the line, several French ships lose roughly sixty to eighty percent of the people actually aboard, leaving guns dismounted and masts shot away. Later casualty figures contrast that destruction with Leander's reported cost of only fourteen wounded and no dead. As each French ship strikes, British fire shifts to the next target and accelerates the collapse.

evidence.note: The transcript details Leander's raking position and casualty levels aboard the French van.
The transcript revisits Leander's attacks and corrects its British casualty figure to fourteen wounded and no dead.

segments.summary: The 50-gun Leander exploits gaps to rake larger French ships while the leading vessels suffer catastrophic crew losses.

segments.title: Aquilon rakes Vanguard and wounds Nelson
segments.body: Aquilon uses its anchor spring to rake Nelson's flagship and inflicts about one hundred casualties, including Nelson's head wound. The maneuver demonstrates the destructive potential of fire running the length of a ship. Nelson initially believes the wound fatal, but returns to the quarterdeck after the surgeon tells him to rest. Aquilon's turn also leaves its bow vulnerable to Minotaur, whose trained crew delivers fire much faster than the French can answer. With many French ships already doubled by two British opponents, the firing-rate advantage can produce roughly four incoming broadsides for every effective French reply.

evidence.note: The transcript describes Aquilon's rake, Nelson's wound, and Minotaur's response.

segments.summary: A single French raking broadside causes almost all Vanguard's casualties, but exposes Aquilon's bow to Minotaur's faster fire.

segments.title: French recognition failures turn fire inward
segments.body: The French rear remains largely inactive while the British roll up the engaged line. Anchor springs, boats, and available crews could have helped those ships shift position or rake the attackers, but their commanders never coordinate such a response. Occasional French fire may have damaged Timoléon's rudder badly enough to contribute to the ship's later scuttling. Farther forward, Peuple Souverain cuts its anchor cable to escape concentrated British fire and drifts south through the darkness. French ships in the rear lack recognition lights, assume the moving hull is British, and fire on their own damaged ship. The contrast with Nelson's illuminated ensigns and mast lights turns night identification from a minor precaution into a visible command-and-control advantage.

evidence.note: The transcript attributes possible rudder damage to French fire and describes rear ships firing on drifting Peuple Souverain in the absence of recognition signals.

segments.summary: Inactive rear ships and absent night-recognition measures leave French fire more dangerous to their own damaged vessels than to the British attack.

segments.title: Command depth keeps damaged British ships in action
segments.body: When Majestic's captain is killed, Lieutenant Robert Cuthbert disentangles the ship, takes a new position, and continues engaging. Naval effectiveness resides in trained crews and a deep command tradition as well as hulls and guns. A familiar maxim contrasts the few years needed to build a ship with roughly thirty years to build a crew and centuries to build an institutional tradition. The comparison with Joseon command failures during the Imjin War shows the danger of political systems repeatedly removing officers whose competence makes them appear threatening. France can replace hulls faster than it can rebuild the experienced people lost through decades of religious exclusion and revolutionary purges. That personnel shortage helps explain why later French strategy depends on obtaining or subordinating Spanish and Dutch naval strength.

evidence.note: The transcript uses Majestic's continued action to explain British command depth and French loss of institutional experience.

segments.summary: British junior officers maneuver and keep fighting after casualties, exposing the institutional gap between the two fleets.

segments.title: Bellerophon holds the 120-gun Orient alone
segments.body: Bellerophon fights Orient alone from the opening phase until about 8 p.m., an engagement a third-rate should not survive against a well-handled 120-gun first-rate. Captain Henry D'Esterre Darby's ship suffers 197 casualties and repeated fires but keeps the French flagship occupied. British fire mortally wounds Admiral Brueys and devastates Orient's quarterdeck before Bellerophon finally cuts her cable and withdraws for repairs. The duel makes the comparison between the fleets concrete: gun count matters only when command, training, and rate of fire can turn those guns into coordinated combat power.

evidence.note: The transcript describes Bellerophon holding Orient alone, the British casualties, Brueys's mortal wound, and the eventual withdrawal for repairs.

segments.summary: A British 74-gun third-rate absorbs the attention of the much larger French flagship for hours, exposing the gap between nominal armament and effective fighting power.

segments.title: Orient burns and explodes at the center of the battle
segments.body: Alexander and Swiftsure arrive after Bellerophon has absorbed a punishing fight against the much larger flagship. Fire appears in Orient's lower gun decks, where powder handling or a weapons-locker explosion may have started it. British gun crews initially direct fire toward the burning areas, hindering French firefighting and feeding the flames. As the fire climbs through the ports, masts, and sails, nearby ships close their gunports, soak their decks, and pull away. At 10 p.m. Orient explodes with enough force to open seams, wound sailors through concussion, and scatter burning wreckage across the anchorage. Survivor testimony is uneven: a French officer picked up by the British supplied an account, while many men who reached shore encountered Bedouin hostility sharpened by the fleet's earlier foraging parties.

evidence.note: The transcript traces the renewed attack, spread of fire, precautions aboard nearby ships, and Orient's explosion.

segments.summary: Fresh British ships renew the attack on Orient before an uncontrolled fire reaches the French flagship's magazine.

segments.title: The battle continues overnight and only four ships escape
segments.body: Franklin and Tonnant continue resistance into the night, while the battle renews after dawn. British ships surround damaged vessels that drift or run aground. The frigate Artémise strikes its flag as Theseus turns toward it, then its crew abandons and burns the ship. If the strike was intended to lure in a boarding party, that deception would later have been treated as a war crime. Villeneuve uses the resistance of the remaining ships to extract Généreux, Guillaume Tell, and two frigates from the anchorage. The rear ships had contributed little to the main action, leaving most of the force captured, destroyed, or scuttled while only four vessels escape.

evidence.note: The transcript follows the overnight resistance, dawn action, captures, scuttling, and Villeneuve's limited escape.

segments.summary: Fighting resumes after Orient's explosion, and Villeneuve ultimately extracts only two ships of the line and two frigates.

segments.title: Measuring the Nile's extraordinary destruction
segments.body: A ship-by-ship calculation supports the higher estimate of roughly five thousand French killed and wounded, plus nearly four thousand captured. France loses eleven of thirteen ships of the line and two of four frigates, amounting to more than three quarters of the seventeen major warships committed. British losses are 218 killed and 677 wounded, but no British ship is lost and even grounded Culloden is recovered. The human cost remains severe on both sides, yet the disparity approaches ten French casualties or prisoners for every British casualty. Comparisons with Trafalgar, Tsushima, and Midway emphasize how exceptional it is to destroy such a large share of an enemy's entire deployed force.

evidence.note: The transcript calculates French casualties and ship losses and compares the scale with other decisive naval battles.

segments.summary: Ship losses and likely casualties place the Nile among the rare fleet battles that annihilated an opponent rather than merely defeating it.

segments.title: Nelson turns battlefield prizes into intelligence
segments.body: Nelson does not treat the last gunfire as the end of the operation. He remains in Aboukir Bay until 16 August, using papers recovered from captured ships to assess the French position in Egypt and prepare reports. British crews also secure damaged prizes and recover Culloden while the strategic news begins its journey across the Mediterranean. Captain Edward Berry's injury leads Nelson to promote Thomas Hardy as his new flag captain. Intelligence work, repair, communication, and personnel decisions convert the tactical victory into an operational result.

evidence.note: The transcript describes the immediate work to free Culloden, secure prizes, and accept the remaining French surrender.
The transcript describes Nelson's two-week stay, use of captured documents, dispatch preparations, and Hardy's promotion as flag captain.

segments.summary: Nelson remains in Aboukir Bay for two weeks to assess captured documents, organize reports, repair the fleet, and reshape his command team.

segments.title: Napoleon is trapped as the Second Coalition expands
segments.body: News reaches Napoleon on 14 August, confirming that his army has lost the maritime support needed to sustain or extract it. He initially blames Rear Admiral Blanquet and inaccurately claims Franklin surrendered undamaged, even though the ship had been devastated in the action. Napoleon eventually returns to France without the army, leaving it trapped in Egypt. International reaction worsens France's strategic position as Russia, Austria, and the Ottoman Empire enter the coalition, making the Nile a defining event before the formal war begins. Seen together, these coalition wars form one continuing Anglo-French struggle conducted through changing groups of allied states. Revolutionary France's emergence also reverses the ideological alignment, leaving Britain to defend much of the existing European order after earlier representing a more commercial and industrial form of modernity.

evidence.note: The transcript describes Napoleon's isolation and the diplomatic expansion of the Second Coalition.

segments.summary: The naval defeat isolates Napoleon's army in Egypt and encourages Russia, Austria, and the Ottoman Empire to join the war against France.

segments.title: Leander's capture delays confirmation of victory in Britain
segments.body: Nelson sends Leander toward St Vincent with his official account of the victory, but the escaped French ship Généreux captures her. Britain therefore does not receive confirmed news until 2 October, delaying the government's ability to exploit the result. Other states react sooner, with Russia, Austria, and the Ottoman Empire joining the struggle against France. Even an annihilating tactical victory still depended on vulnerable ships to carry strategic information across the Mediterranean.

evidence.note: The transcript identifies Généreux as Leander's captor, notes Britain's delayed confirmation, and describes the coalition response.

segments.summary: The escaped French ship Généreux captures Nelson's dispatch carrier, slowing British exploitation even as other powers react to the Nile.

segments.title: Prize money reveals the battle's commercial value
segments.body: The captured fleet produces about £130,000 in prize money, while the British Parliament grants Nelson £2,000 a year for life. The Irish Parliament adds £1,000 annually until the Act of Union ends that separate payment, and the East India Company awards another £10,000. Those rewards reflect the battle's commercial value to London, Liverpool, and other trading centers as well as Nelson's personal glory. Napoleon's presence in Egypt does not stop British commerce, because merchants route cargo around the Cape and adjust freight charges to the risk. Operational success in the Mediterranean therefore affected state finance, private trade, and the incentives of the age-of-sail navy.

evidence.note: The transcript lists prize money, parliamentary income, and the East India Company's reward to Nelson.

segments.summary: Naval prize money and East India Company rewards show how closely victory, trade protection, and personal fortune were linked.
